Spatial multiomics: downstream experiments after integration

In this presentation, the spatial multiomics data are reviewed first. After that, the downstream experiments run after integration in 60 papers from 2025 and 2026 are reviewed: what each experiment does, on which data, and with which metric; each scoring method is explained right after the first task that uses it. This version keeps 10 of the 46 tasks: the hardest and least used of those that the outputs of our model and our data can support.

Thanh Bui  /  University of Central Florida  /  Fall 2026 Press → to begin  /  ? for controls
This version of Part 2 is scoped to our model: of the 46 tasks, it shows 10 of the 13 whose inputs our model already saves (joint embedding, predicted domains, per-modality embeddings and variances, modality weights, transport maps between sections) and that our data can support, the hardest and least used ones, with the method notes that go with them. Part 1 covered the data and the models. This part first reviews the data, then the downstream experiments run after integration, paper by paper. Every number on a slide comes from a record with its figure.
01DataSample, section and spot

Data units: sample, section and spot

Throughout this presentation, three nested units are used:

NoteIt should be noted that modality counts are per spot within one section, while section and sample counts are reported separately, e.g., HTAN has 131 sections from 78 cases.

Clicks: 1: Each time point is a new sample: a different animal, or a new biopsy. 2: A sample's tissue block is cut into thin sections, each placed on a glass slide. 3: The assay tiles each section with spots, or pixels, 10 to 100 µm wide. 4: Every molecule read in a spot carries that spot's barcode, whatever its modality. 5 to 9: Over time, the number of modalities read per spot increases: 1 in 2016, 2 in 2020, and 5 in 2025; the box steps through one assay per click. The clicks: ST (Ståhl et al., Science 2016), RNA only; DBiT-seq (Liu et al., Cell 2020), RNA + 22 proteins; spatial ATAC–RNA and CUT&Tag–RNA (Zhang et al., Nature 2023) and MISAR-seq (Jiang et al., Nat. Methods 2023), RNA + ATAC or one histone mark, one pair per section; Spatial-DMT (Lee et al., Nature 2025), RNA + DNA methylation, down to 10 µm; Spatial-Mux-seq (Guo et al., Nat. Methods 2025), ATAC, H3K27me3, H3K27ac, RNA and 122 proteins in the same pixels. Our LPC data (spatial tri-omics, Zhang et al., Nature 2025) read 3 per spot. Sample: one biological specimen, i.e. one animal or donor at one time point or condition; one sample can give one or several sections. Section (slice): one thin slice cut from a sample's tissue block and placed on one glass slide. Spot (pixel): one capture site on the section, from 100 µm (ST) and 55 µm (Visium) down to 20 or 10 µm (DBiT-based assays); each spot is one row of every count matrix. In animal studies, collecting a sample ends the animal: in the tri-omics paper, where our LPC data come from, animals were randomized to time-point groups and euthanized at each collection, so P0 to P21 and 5, 10 and 21 days post-lesion are different mice (Methods). The same person can be sampled again only in biopsy studies, e.g. a HER2+ gastric cancer trial with three biopsies per patient (Clin Cancer Res 2025), and each biopsy is a new piece of tissue. A frozen block can be cut again later, but that gives more sections of the same time point. (≈2:00)
01DataModalities: raw to processed

Modalities: raw to processed

For each modality, the raw data given by the assay and the processed data used in our experiments are summarized as follows:

ModalityRaw: what the assay givesProcessed: what we use
RNASpot × gene countsX_pca_sct: normalized, then principal components
ATACFragments, then spot × peak countsX_lsi_ccre: dimension-reduced counts, and X_spectral: spectral embedding
Histone marksFragments, then spot × peak counts, for each markActivating: H3K27ac, H3K4me3 (genes switched on)
Repressive: H3K27me3 (genes kept off)		X_lsi_ccre (H3K27ac) or X_spectral_scaled (H3K27me3, H3K4me3), plus X_spectral
ProteinSpot × antibody counts, plus isotype controlsX_pca
ImageTissue image, H&E or brightfieldX_image_embedding: one image embedding per spot

NoteIt should be noted that every processed matrix keeps one row per spot. Hence, the modalities of one section stay aligned by the spot barcode.

One row per modality: what the assay gives, then what our models read. RNA: spot × gene counts, normalized, then principal components (X_pca_sct). ATAC: fragments are counted into spot × peak counts, then reduced to X_lsi_ccre; X_spectral is a spectral embedding of the same counts. Histone marks differ in what they do: H3K27ac marks active enhancers and promoters and H3K4me3 marks active promoters, so both go with genes being switched on, while H3K27me3, laid down by the Polycomb complex, marks genes being kept off, i.e., repressed. Their counts follow the ATAC route: X_lsi_ccre for H3K27ac, X_spectral_scaled for H3K27me3 and H3K4me3, plus X_spectral. Protein: spot × antibody counts, with isotype controls in the lymph-node panel, reduced to X_pca. Image: the tissue image, H&E (MISAR-seq) or brightfield (P22, tri-omics), gives one embedding per spot (X_image_embedding; X_image_embedding_local for the H&E images). All processed data come from the v2 files on MinIO. Click 1: the Note. (≈1:30)
01DataSpot size

Spatial resolution: smaller spots, more modalities

Over the years, the spot size has decreased from 100 µm (about 3–30 cells) to 10 µm (about one cell), while the number of modalities per section has increased:

100 µm spots / 1 modality / ST, 2016
55 µm spots / 2 modalities / Visium lymph node data
20 µm pixels / 2–3 modalities / P22 ATAC–RNA, 2023; tri-omics, 2025
10 µm pixels / 2 modalities / DBiT-seq, 2020; Spatial-DMT, 2025

Sizes: Rao et al., Nature 2021 (ST 100 µm, Visium 55 µm); Vickovic et al., Nat. Methods 2019 ("100 µm (3–30 cells)"); assay papers in the notes of slide 2, plus Rodriques et al., Science 2019 (Slide-seq), Deng et al., Nature 2022 and Science 2022, Long et al., Nat. Methods 2024, Enninful et al., Nat. Methods 2026 (DBiTplus).

Same 1 mm square each time; each click swaps in a finer grid, and each sheet in the stack is one modality measured on the same section. RNA is always the base sheet: 1 sheet for ST, 2 for the Visium lymph node data (RNA, protein), up to 3 at 20 µm (P22 ATAC–RNA has RNA and ATAC; tri-omics adds about 150 proteins, with ATAC or H3K27me3), and 2 at 10 µm (DBiT-seq adds protein; Spatial-DMT adds DNA methylation). So the stack grows while the spots shrink. ST spots are 100 µm, roughly 3 to 30 cells. Visium is 55 µm; the lymph node data we use is Visium CytAssist with RNA and a 35-antibody panel. The deterministic-barcoding assays reach 20 µm and then 10 µm, about one cell. The chart on the right puts every assay on one axis: smaller is lower, bigger markers read more modalities. Note size is not spacing; I drew spacing at twice the size. (≈2:30)

*Type 2 is not covered in this talk. It should be noted that type 1 labels each spot (e.g., domains and gradients), while type 4 relates cells and domains to one another and over time (e.g., niches, neighbours, trajectories and clones). Tags: the output of our model that each task reads; "domains" are its predicted domains. Tasks: downstream-task atlas of 46 tasks and 49 primary sources, 2024 to 10 November 2026.

Each click enlarges one type in the middle and blurs the others; the next click puts it back. Type 1 (7 tasks) is what every integration paper shows: embeddings, domains, labels, deconvolution, plus atlases and registration across sections; e.g., SpatialGlue, MISO, SpaMosaic, SANTO. Type 2 (7 tasks) predicts values that were not measured: imputation, histology-to-molecule, interpolation, super-resolution; e.g., SpaMosaic, SpatialEx, spaVAE, CORAL. Type 3 (12 tasks, the largest) asks which features differ and what regulates them, from differential tests to element-to-gene links and regulatory networks; e.g., SEPAR, SpaMV, MultiGATE, SpaDC. Type 4 (7 tasks) is about relations: neighbours, ligand–receptor signalling, niches, trajectories and clones; e.g., NicheCompass, COSMOS, LIANA+. Type 5 (6 tasks) needs extra data: patient labels, survival, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) or CRISPR screens; only 2 of its 12 papers run the experiment, and the others are adjacent. Type 6 (7 tasks) audits or extends the model: uncertainty, open-set rejection, modality contribution, retrieval. In-silico perturbation sits here, not in type 5, since editing the input tests model sensitivity rather than a biological intervention. The task slides then follow in reverse order, from type 6 back to type 1. Of the 13 tasks that our model can feed with what it already saves, and that our data can support, this version keeps the 10 hardest and least used; the blue tag names the output each task reads. Integrated embedding, domain clustering and differential expression also fit, but are left out: they are the easiest checks and the ones most papers already show. Joint embedding: the per-spot joint posterior mean, saved as the embedding table. Domains: the predicted domains, i.e., Mclust labels on the joint embedding, which serve as the groups of every type 3 test, run on the measured data. Multi-slice fit: one model over an ordered list of sections, which may hold different modalities. Transport maps: the top-k unbalanced optimal-transport coupling between adjacent sections, saved per pair. Posterior variance: the per-spot variance of each modality's embedding, saved with its mean. Modality embeddings: one embedding per modality in one space. Modality weights: the aggregator weight of each modality per spot when the joint embedding is formed. Type 2 is not covered in this talk, as the footnote says: our model computes reconstructions from the joint embedding, and of one modality from the others, but does not save them, and with the current best configurations they are in the reduced space, e.g., principal components, not gene counts. Type 5 has no task here either: our data have no patient cohorts, genetic association statistics or perturbation screens. In type 3, differential accessibility stands for the tests between predicted domains; expression, abundance, spatial variability and enrichment follow the same pattern. Within each type, the tasks run from the hardest to the easiest, i.e., from the weakest ground truth and most assumptions to the most direct check. On every task card, the ground truth is a reference the model never saw, and the model works through an embedding, i.e., the short vector it learns for each spot. (≈3:00)
02ExperimentsType 6 / Uncertainty maps

Uncertainty maps: where to trust the model

Given the embeddings, an uncertainty score is computed for each spot and then checked against held-out values:

Question
Where in the tissue should the model be trusted less?
Input / data
Measured profiles per spot, with some values held outGround truth: Held-out measured values, whose error the score should predict
Input / model
An uncertainty score per spot, i.e., one number where higher means less certainE.g., posterior spread or modality disagreement; not a probability
Output
An uncertainty map, then the spots to trust, set by a cut-offThe legend must state what the score measures
Scored by
Error and modality disagreement where the score is high, e.g., in SCIGMARecommended: Calibration, error against score, and unseen sections
Papers
SCIGMA

Task: downstream-task atlas, T40 "Spatial uncertainty and reliability maps". Papers: SCIGMA, Nat. Genet. 2026.

This is the most novel task of type 6, and SCIGMA, published in September 2026, is its only demonstration. In this slide, the task is presented in three steps. First, the input consists of the measured profiles, with some values held out from training. Given the embeddings, the model gives each spot an uncertainty score, which is defined as one number per spot with no unit, where higher means less certain. In other words, the score ranks spots against each other, and it is not a probability. In SCIGMA, the score is a temperature learned for each spot, which is high where the modalities of that spot are hard to align. Click 1: the output is an uncertainty map; here, the score is high at domain borders, where spots mix two domains, and in a damaged patch. Click 2: after that, with a cut-off fixed in advance, the most uncertain spots are set aside, and the rest are trusted. Click 3: finally, the score is checked in three ways; the next slide presents how the score is obtained from the embeddings, and the one after it how the two plots are read, first on trained sections and then on an unseen one. Specifically, the first check is whether the score ranks the errors: spots with a higher score should have a larger error on held-out values, which SCIGMA checks at its 1% to 20% most uncertain locations. In SCIGMA's mouse-brain data, the map is highest in the lateral ventricle, the lateral preoptic area and parts of the cortex, i.e., regions named from the Allen atlas, where RNA and ATAC disagree more and the reconstruction error is larger. In addition, the score rises when noise is added on purpose. The second check is calibration: if the model states that an interval holds 90% of values, about 90% of held-out values should fall in it, and points below the diagonal mean that the model is overconfident. The third check repeats both on a section left out of training, since the score is needed most on new tissue; the slide after next draws it in orange. It should be noted that a score is not a probability until it is calibrated, that the error must be measured against held-out data rather than the model's own denoised values, which would be circular, and that high uncertainty can also reflect real biological variation, as SCIGMA's authors warn. (≈2:00)
02ExperimentsMethod note / Uncertainty maps

Three ways to obtain an uncertainty score

Given the embeddings, one number per spot can be obtained in three ways, which are defined as follows:

Posterior spread

\[ u_i = \frac{1}{d}\, \lVert \sigma_i \rVert_2^2 \]where \(\sigma_i \in \mathbb{R}^d\) holds spot \(i\)'s standard deviation on each of the \(d\) axes
  • Key idea: The encoder places each spot with a mean and a spread,
  • Large spread: The data at the spot are ambiguous,
  • Output: One map per modality, or for the joint embedding.

Modality disagreement

\[ u_i = 1 - \cos\big(\mu_i^{\mathrm{RNA}}, \mu_i^{\mathrm{ATAC}}\big) \]where \(\mu_i^{m}\) is spot \(i\)'s embedding from modality \(m\) alone
  • Key idea: Each modality embeds the same spot on its own,
  • Far apart: The modalities disagree at the spot,
  • Example: SCIGMA learns this as a temperature per spot,
  • Caveat: A loss between modalities lowers it, a loss to the joint only bounds it.

Rerun disagreement

\[ u_i = 1 - \operatorname{mean}_{s<t}\, \frac{|N_i^s \cap N_i^t|}{|N_i^s \cup N_i^t|} \]where \(N_i^s\) is the set of \(k\) nearest neighbours of spot \(i\) in run \(s\)
  • Key idea: The model is trained again with other seeds,
  • Changing neighbours: The spot's place is unstable,
  • Advantage: Neighbours need no alignment between runs.
In this slide, three ways to obtain an uncertainty score from the embeddings are presented, and the next slide shows how the score is checked. Throughout the slide, spot A, in blue, is certain, and spot B, in orange, is uncertain. First, the posterior spread: a variational encoder gives each spot not a point but a mean and a variance on every axis of the embedding, drawn here as a dot and an ellipse. The score u_i is then defined as the variance averaged over the d axes, i.e., the squared L2 norm of the vector of standard deviations sigma_i, divided by d. In other words, a large spread means that the encoder cannot place the spot, i.e., the data at the spot are ambiguous. This score is available for each modality's embedding and for the joint embedding, and it is the only one of the three that states a spread. Click 1: after that, the modality disagreement: each modality also embeds the spot on its own, in the same shared space, so the RNA and ATAC embeddings of one spot can be compared. The score is defined as one minus their cosine similarity, which is 0.00 for spot A and 0.52 for spot B in the toy, computed from the drawn points. SCIGMA learns a version of this score: a small network predicts a temperature for each spot from its combined embedding, and its alignment loss raises the temperature where the spot's own RNA and ATAC embeddings match it no better than those of other spots do. Consequently, the temperature is high where the modalities disagree. It should be noted that the training loss changes what this score means. If the modalities are aligned with a contrastive loss between them, the score is lowered for every trained spot, down to a floor set by the gap that such losses leave between modalities, so only its ranking carries meaning, and its values cannot be compared across models. If each modality is aligned with the joint embedding instead, as in SCIGMA, the score is only bounded, since the angle between the two modalities is at most the sum of their angles to the joint embedding, and it keeps more signal. Click 2: finally, the rerun disagreement: the model is trained again with other seeds, and for each spot, the k nearest neighbours in the embedding of each run are compared. The score is defined as one minus the mean Jaccard overlap, i.e., the shared neighbours over all neighbours, across pairs of runs. In the toy, spot A keeps the same four neighbours, so its score is 0.00, while spot B keeps one of four, so its score is 1 minus 1/7, i.e., 0.86. It should be noted that comparing neighbours rather than coordinates avoids aligning the embedding spaces of different runs. Overall, none of these numbers is a probability: each only ranks spots, so each must be checked against an error that can be measured, which the next slide presents. (≈2:30)
02ExperimentsMethod note / Uncertainty maps

Reading the two checks on the uncertainty map

Given the score \(u_i\) of the previous slide, the two plots are built on trained sections, then on an unseen section \(S'\):

Held-out error by score \(u_i\)

\[ \mathrm{RMSE}_b = \frac{\lVert x_{H_b} - \hat{x}_{H_b} \rVert_2}{\sqrt{|H_b|}}, \quad H_b = \{\, (i,g) \in H : i \in B_b \,\} \]where \(H\) is the set of entries hidden in training, and \(x_{H_b}\), \(\hat{x}_{H_b}\) the true and predicted values \(x_{ig}\), \(\hat{x}_{ig}\) on \(H_b\)
  • How to build: Split \(u_i\) into five equal ranges \(B_1, \dots, B_5\), one bar per bin,
  • Useful score: The bars fall from \(B_1\) to \(B_5\); at random, they sit on the dashed line,
  • Unseen \(S'\): Every entry is hidden; the bars rise, but still fall.

Calibration, from the posterior spread

\[ I_{ig}(p) = \hat{x}_{ig} \pm z_p \hat{\sigma}_{ig}, \quad C(p) = \frac{\#\{\, (i,g) \in H : x_{ig} \in I_{ig}(p) \,\}}{|H|}, \quad \text{ideal: } C(p) = p \]where \(\hat{\sigma}_{ig}\) is the spread of feature \(g\) over decoded samples \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma_i^2)\)
  • Each dot: A stated level \(p\); \(C(p)\) tells how much of the true values its intervals hold,
  • Below the diagonal: Intervals are too narrow, i.e., overconfident; above it, too wide,
  • Unseen \(S'\): Honest on trained sections, overconfident on \(S'\).
In this slide, the two plots at the end of the uncertainty-map slide are read in turn, with the score u_i of the previous slide as the input. Each plot is built twice: first on entries hidden inside the trained sections, in blue, and then on an unseen section S-prime, in orange. The toy numbers are computed from 500 spots in each. First, the held-out error by score: the scores are split into five equal ranges, from B1, 0.8 to 1.0, down to B5, 0.0 to 0.2, and each bar is the error of the spots in one range. With held-out values, the error is the RMSE, which is defined as follows: before training, a set H of entries is hidden, e.g., 10% of the gene values, where entry (i, g) is feature g at spot i. For every hidden entry of the spots in the bin, the true value x_ig is compared with the predicted value x-hat_ig, decoded from the embedding; the squared differences are averaged, and the square root is taken. In other words, it is the L2 norm of the errors in the bin, divided by the square root of their number. In the toy, each spot has one hidden entry. When only the embeddings are saved, the error that can be measured is e_b, the share of spots in the bin whose predicted domain differs from the true domain; the true domains are used only to score, never to fit. In the toy, the blue bars fall from 1.32 in B1 to 0.43 in B5, which suggests that u_i ranks the errors. The dashed line is the RMSE of all trained spots, 0.92; a random score would put every bar near it, and bars that rise instead would mean that the score is reversed. All three scores of the previous slide can be checked this way, and SCIGMA reports a close version, the RMSE at its 1%, 5%, 10% and 20% most uncertain locations. Click 1: after that, the calibration plot, which needs more than a ranking: it needs an interval on each predicted value, and only the posterior spread gives one, through the decoder. In other words, for spot i, embeddings z are drawn from the normal with mean mu_i and variance sigma_i squared, each is decoded, and the spread of the decoded values of feature g is sigma-hat_ig. The interval at level p is then the predicted value x-hat_ig plus or minus z_p times sigma-hat_ig, chosen so that it should hold the true value with chance p. For each stated level p, from 50% to 95%, C(p) is defined as the share of hidden entries whose true value falls inside its interval, and the point is placed at p across and C(p) up. A calibrated model lies on the dashed diagonal; points below it mean intervals that are too narrow, i.e., an overconfident model, and points above it mean intervals wider than needed. In the toy, the blue curve lies near the diagonal: a stated 90% interval holds 89% of the hidden values. It should be noted that very wide intervals pass this plot while saying little, so their width is reported too. Click 2: finally, both checks are repeated on an unseen section S-prime, e.g., another slice, animal or stage, which is kept out of training entirely, so every entry of it is held out. Inside a trained section, a hidden entry still has its spot's other values and its neighbours in training, so the blue checks are the easy ones. In the toy, the scores on S-prime are higher, with a mean of 0.65 against 0.50, and no spot falls in B5. The orange bars are higher than the blue ones but still fall, from 2.14 to 1.21, so the score still ranks the errors. However, the orange curve lies below the diagonal: a stated 90% interval holds only 67% of the true values. Consequently, the model is honest on the sections it was trained on but overconfident on new tissue, which is the usual way calibration breaks under a shift. Overall, both colours are reported, never the blue one alone. (≈2:30)
02ExperimentsType 6 / Modality contribution

Modality contribution: which data the model uses

How much each modality contributes to a named result is measured, per spot and per predicted domain:

Question
Which modality drives a given result, and where?
Input / data
Two or more modalities per spot, and a result fixed in advanceGround truth: True domains annotated by hand, or a simulated signal
Input / model
Weights or retrained models, and predicted domainsA weight is a model coefficient, not a share of the biology
Output
Weights per spot and domain, then the score lost against true domains without a modalityMasking a trained model is not the same as retraining
Scored by
Attention weights and component ablations, e.g., in SpatialGlueRecommended: added noise and the same tuning for every ablation
Papers
SpatialGlue / SpaMV
Caveat
A non-linear weight sets a linear mixSpatialGlue: a softmax of a tanh score, then a weighted average

Task: downstream-task atlas, T45 "Modality and feature contribution analysis". Papers: SpatialGlue, Nat. Methods 2024; SpaMV, Nat. Commun. 2026.

This is the most popular task of type 6: it is the only one with two demonstrating papers, SpatialGlue and SpaMV. On every task card, the ground truth is a reference the model never saw, and the model works through an embedding, i.e., the short vector it learns for each spot. The question must name a result, e.g., the predicted domains, since a modality can matter for one result and not another. The input is two or more modalities and that fixed result; the model supplies attention weights, factor loadings, or versions of itself retrained without a modality. Click 0: in a two-modality model, each spot gets an RNA weight, and the ATAC weight is the rest. In SpatialGlue on P22 mouse brain, RNA weighs more in the corpus callosum, a white-matter tract, and ATAC more in cortex; this toy copies that direction, but its values are made up. Click 1: averaged per predicted domain, the weights give one bar each; SpatialGlue averages them over its own clusters, named afterwards by anatomy, e.g., the cortex and the lateral ventricle. Click 2: an ablation retrains the model without one modality, with the same tuning budget, and records the score lost against the true domains, i.e., expert labels; here both modalities together beat either alone. Masking a modality in a model that was trained with it measures something else, since the model never saw that input missing. Click 3: the atlas recommends adding noise to one modality; a sound model then trusts that modality less. SpatialGlue reports its weights and component ablations, and SpaMV reads contributions from shared and private factors. It should be noted that SpatialGlue computes its weights from the embeddings, not from the raw counts, and that two redundant modalities can each look unimportant when removed alone. The last row is a further caveat, the mix of non-linear and linear steps: in SpatialGlue, each weight is a softmax over modalities of a tanh score on the spot's embeddings, so it is a non-linear function of them, whereas the combined embedding is a weighted average, i.e., linear in the two embeddings once the weights are fixed. As the weights depend on the same embeddings they multiply, the combination as a whole is still non-linear; moreover, the paper describes encoders with a ReLU activation, while the released code applies none, so there each modality's embedding is linear in its input. (≈2:20)
02ExperimentsType 6 / Cross-modal retrieval

Cross-modal retrieval: finding the measured pair

Given the embeddings of two modalities, the candidates of one are ranked for each query spot of the other and checked against its measured pair:

Question
Does a spot's embedding in one modality find the same spot in another?
Input / data
Two modalities per spot, so the pairs are knownGround truth: The measured pair, in a pool from one true domain
Input / model
An embedding per modality in one shared space, and a similarity, e.g., cosineCaveat: A contrastive loss trains this ranking, directly between modalities, indirectly via the joint
Output
Candidates ranked per query, then the rank of each true matchThe size and make-up of the pool set the difficulty
Scored by
Top-k precision on held-out patients, e.g., in spEMORecommended: Both directions, pools from one true domain, and a random baseline
Papers
spEMO

Task: downstream-task atlas, T42 "Cross-modal retrieval and correspondence ranking". Papers: spEMO, Nat. Biomed. Eng. 2026.

In this slide, cross-modal retrieval is presented, which tests whether the embeddings of two modalities line up, without decoding any molecule. First, the input consists of spots with two modalities measured on them, here an image patch and an RNA profile, so the true pairs are known. Given the embeddings, the model places both modalities in one shared space, and the similarity of two embeddings is defined as, e.g., the cosine of the angle between them. Click 1: after that, for the ringed query spot, the candidate RNA profiles are ranked by their similarity to its image patch; in the toy, the true match comes third, behind two spots from the same domain. Click 2: over many queries, the output is the rank of each true match, and a query is defined as a hit when its match falls within the top k, i.e., the first k candidates. Click 3: finally, the hit rate is scored, and it depends on the pool. In other words, candidates from a broad pool are easy to tell apart, candidates from the same domain are hard, and random retrieval sets the floor; consequently, both directions, pools from one true domain and a random baseline are recommended. Specifically, spEMO introduces this task as a benchmark for pathology image models: on public spatial transcriptomics data from ten diseases, split by patient, it trains an RNA encoder to match each image model's embeddings, and it reports a cross-entropy loss and the top-1 and top-10 precision. No image model reaches a high top-1 precision, which the authors relate to spots of similar function having similar profiles. It should be noted that the training loss matters: if the two modalities are aligned with a contrastive loss between them, the ranking is the training objective, since the loss is a softmax over the same candidates, so retrieval on trained spots is circular and must be scored on held-out sections; if each modality is aligned with the joint embedding instead, as in SCIGMA, retrieval from the joint embedding is trained directly, and retrieval between the modalities only indirectly. In addition, neighbouring patches and serial sections can make near-duplicate candidates, and that a good rank says nothing about how accurately any molecule is predicted. Overall, retrieval checks that the embeddings of two modalities are aligned, not what they predict. (≈2:00)
02ExperimentsType 4 / Fate mapping

Fate mapping: from earlier to later cells

Cells measured at two real times are matched by optimal transport, i.e., a plan that moves the earlier cells onto the later ones at the lowest total cost:

Question
Which earlier cells become which later cells, and how sure is that?
Input / data
Cells from two or more real times, with batch labelsGround truth: Lineage barcodes, or a held-out middle time
Input / model
A shared embedding; the cost is the distance in itCaveat: A loss on pairs of consecutive times returns its own pairs and can erase the real change
Output
A transport plan per interval, then a fate probability per earlier cellA match of populations, not traced ancestry
Scored by
Known transitions and a knockout of a predicted driver, e.g., in moscotRecommended: lineage barcodes, held-out times and other costs
Papers
moscot (adjacent) / brain tri-omics atlas (enabling)

Task: downstream-task atlas, T31 "Temporal fate mapping and population transitions with transport". Papers: moscot, Nature 2025 (adjacent); brain tri-omics atlas (spatial ARP-seq and CTRP-seq), Nature 2025 (enabling).

Fate mapping links cells measured at real times, which, unlike an order inferred from one time point, gives the direction. Collecting a sample ends the animal, so no cell is seen twice; optimal transport instead finds a plan that moves the earlier population onto the later one at the lowest total cost, where the cost is the distance between cells in the embedding. The input is cells from two or more times with batch labels; the model supplies the shared embedding and so the cost. Click 1: the transport plan for one interval; each row is an earlier cell, each column a later cell, and a stronger blue means more of that cell is sent there. Click 2: summing each row over the later fates gives a fate probability per earlier cell. Click 3: the check predicts a held-out middle time and compares its state shares with the measured ones; a close match supports the plan but does not prove ancestry. moscot, adjacent here, maps 1.7 million mouse-embryo cells across 20 time points as well as a method built for that atlas; on pancreas RNA and ATAC from E14.5 to E16.5, it predicts that delta and epsilon cells branch off endocrine progenitors at a similar state, and a NEUROD2 knockout in human stem-cell islets then reduced the ghrelin-producing epsilon cells. The brain tri-omics atlas, enabling here, supplies six postnatal ages. It should be noted that the embedding must not be trained on the same transport: if pairs of consecutive times, e.g., from a plan computed in advance, are pulled together during training, the plan computed afterwards largely returns those pairs, so the fate probabilities restate the training matches rather than adding evidence. In addition, such a loss is easiest to satisfy by removing what differs between times, i.e., the real change, and a time used in any training pair can no longer serve as the held-out middle time. Consequently, the check must use a time point, or lineage barcodes, kept out of every training pair. Furthermore, cells divide and die between times, so a plan that keeps every cell's mass can invent transitions, and a sharper plan is not a better one. (≈2:00)
02ExperimentsMethod note / Fate mapping

Optimal transport: the plan and its checks

The fate-mapping slide relies on an optimal transport plan, which is made and checked as follows:

Cost and plan

  • Cost matrix: distance between each earlier and later cell in the embedding
  • Plan: how much of each earlier cell goes to each later cell
  • Rows and columns sum to the cell shares; the total cost is lowest

Blur, growth and death

  • Entropic term: blurs the plan, so each cell spreads its mass; faster to solve
  • Unbalanced: row sums may change, for growth and death
  • Growth and death rates come from marker genes

A held-out middle time

  • Interpolate: move the earlier cells part-way along the plan
  • Score: distance between predicted and measured cells; lower is better
  • Lineage barcodes: heritable tags that trace real ancestry, a stronger truth
This slide explains the transport plan behind fate mapping. Left: the cost matrix holds the distance between every earlier cell and every later cell in the shared embedding, and the plan says how much of each earlier cell is sent to each later cell. Each row of the plan sums to that earlier cell's share of the population and each column to the later cell's share; among all such plans, optimal transport picks the one with the lowest total cost. Click 1: an entropic term is usually added; it blurs the plan so that each cell spreads its mass over several later cells, and makes it fast to solve. Unbalanced transport lets the row sums change: a cell that divides sends more mass, and one that dies sends less. Click 2: the usual check holds out a middle time, moves the earlier cells part-way along the plan, and measures the distance between the predicted and the measured cells, e.g., the cost of the cheapest plan between them; lineage barcodes, i.e., heritable tags read out later, are a stronger truth. moscot computes the cost in a shared latent space, e.g., PCA for RNA and LSI for ATAC, adds the entropic term, and handles growth and death with rates from proliferation and apoptosis genes and soft penalties on the shares. It scores plans on the mouse-embryo atlas by the share of transitions that stay within a germ layer or match a curated list, and on pancreas shows that the cost matters: squared Euclidean and cosine costs gave an implausible transition that a geodesic cost did not. It should be noted that matching the shares at a middle time does not prove which cell came from which. (≈2:00)
02ExperimentsType 4 / Trajectory inference

Trajectories: ordering cells along a process

Pseudotime is a cell's relative position along an inferred process, e.g., progenitor to mature oligodendrocyte; it orders cells but is not a clock:

Question
In what order do cells mature from progenitors, and which features change along that order?
Input / data
Maturing cells' profiles, positions, and ages if sampledGround truth: True ages and domains, lineage-tracing barcodes, or simulations
Input / model
The embedding, and a root in a predicted domain, set by markersThe embedding has no built-in direction
Output
An order of cells from the root, then pseudotime per cell and the features that change along itPseudotime is a rank, not days or maturity
Scored by
Agreement with annotated anatomy and genes along the order, e.g., in COSMOSRecommended: Held-out ages, lineage labels, and other roots
Papers
COSMOS / CANDIES / brain tri-omics atlas (enabling)

Task: downstream-task atlas, T30 "Developmental trajectories, pseudotime and changing molecular programs". Papers: COSMOS, Nat. Commun. 2025; CANDIES, Adv. Sci. 2026; brain tri-omics atlas (spatial ARP-seq and CTRP-seq), Nature 2025 (enabling).

A trajectory orders cells along a process, here progenitors becoming mature oligodendrocytes, and pseudotime is each cell's relative position on that order. The input is the profiles of one lineage, and true ages where several were sampled; the model supplies the embedding, and a root, i.e., the starting cell, is chosen from known markers, because the embedding has no built-in direction. Click 1: in the embedding, the cells lie on a path leaving the root. Click 2: the output is pseudotime per cell, mapped back onto the section, and then the genes or peaks that change along it. Click 3: the check uses true ages the model never saw: cells from older animals should sit later. In addition, two other references can be used. Lineage tracing is defined as marking progenitor cells with a heritable label, e.g., a DNA barcode, so that every descendant carries it and the real ancestry can be read later. Simulations generate cells along a path that is known in advance, so the true order of every cell is known by construction. COSMOS runs diffusion pseudotime on its embedding of the P22 mouse-brain ATAC and RNA sections, with the root at the first cell of one of its own predicted clusters, in the caudoputamen, and compares the order with its annotated anatomy by eye; it then selects 577 genes correlated with it, enriched for neurogenesis; its order follows anatomy, which shows the risk, since in one section of one age, position in the tissue can pass for development. CANDIES builds the same kind of map on human skin RNA and protein, with values rising from the dermis toward the pilosebaceous unit, in line with the known order of development. The brain tri-omics atlas, enabling here, measures six postnatal ages from P0 to P21 and finds ATAC signal preceding RNA more often for oligodendrocyte genes than for neuron genes. It should be noted that pseudotime is a rank, not a clock or a probability of fate, and that genes selected along an order cannot also confirm it. (≈2:00)
02ExperimentsMethod note / Trajectory inference

Pseudotime: how it is computed and checked

The trajectory slide relies on a pseudotime per cell, which is computed and checked as follows:

A graph and a root

  • Neighbour graph: Each cell is linked to its nearest cells in the embedding,
  • Root: A start cell is chosen from known markers,
  • Pseudotime: The distance from the root along the graph.

Rank agreement with age

\[ \rho = \operatorname{corr}\big(\operatorname{rank}(p), \operatorname{rank}(a)\big) \]\[ \tau_b = \frac{n_c - n_d}{\sqrt{(n_0 - n_p)(n_0 - n_a)}} \]where \(p_i\) is the pseudotime of cell \(i\) and \(a_i\) its true age; \(n_c\), \(n_d\) count the pairs in and out of order, \(n_0\) all pairs, and \(n_p\), \(n_a\) the pairs tied in \(p\) and in \(a\)
  • True age: The sampling day of each cell, unseen by the model,
  • Output: One number per section in \([-1, 1]\); near 1, pseudotime follows age,
  • Use: Compare models, roots and neighbour counts, not against 1.

Genes along pseudotime

  • Changing genes: Correlated with pseudotime, above a cut-off,
  • Circular: The same counts built the order, so genes follow it by design,
  • Better: Test on another section, or against true ages.
This slide explains how pseudotime is made and checked. Left: each dot is a cell in the embedding, linked to its nearest cells, which gives a neighbour graph. A root, i.e., the starting cell, is chosen from known markers, and pseudotime is the distance from the root along the graph; diffusion pseudotime, the common choice, measures this distance with random walks on the graph, so one noisy link matters less. Click 1: after that, with true ages that the model never saw, e.g., animals sampled on different days, the check is a rank correlation between the pseudotime p_i of each cell and its true age a_i. Spearman's rho is defined as the correlation of the ranks of p with the ranks of a, where cells of the same age share their average rank. Kendall's tau-b looks at pairs of cells: n_c pairs are in the same order in both, n_d in opposite orders, and their difference is divided by a count of the pairs that are not tied, so that the many pairs of cells from one age do not count; the orange pair is one of the n_d. Both give one number per section between minus 1 and 1: near 1, pseudotime follows age; near 0, it is unrelated to age; below 0, the root is likely at the wrong end. Only the order matters, so pseudotime need not be in days. In addition, age is coarse, since older animals still have progenitors, so even a perfect order stays below 1; consequently, the number is used to compare models, roots and numbers of neighbours on the same cells, and not against 1. Click 2: genes that change along pseudotime are usually found by correlating each gene with it. On the section that built the order, many genes follow it by design, since their counts made the embedding; on another section, the same gene follows it more loosely. COSMOS runs diffusion pseudotime in Scanpy on its embedding of the P22 mouse-brain section, with the root at the first cell of one caudoputamen cluster, and keeps the 577 genes whose Pearson correlation with pseudotime has a p-value below 10⁻¹⁰; CANDIES also sets the root by hand, e.g., the dermis in skin, and selects genes by Pearson correlation. Neither has true ages; the brain tri-omics atlas, with six ages from P0 to P21, could supply them. It should be noted that another root or another number of neighbours can reorder the cells, so the check should be repeated with other roots. (≈2:00)
02ExperimentsType 3 / Cross-omics association

Cross-omics links: agreement and disagreement

Matched modalities are compared spot by spot, and the places where they disagree are mapped:

Question
Do two modalities agree, and where do they not?
Input / data
Matched RNA and protein, ATAC or metabolites per spot, and true domains if annotatedGround truth: None; simulated pairs, known controls and new specimens score
Input / model
Predicted domains, cell types or shared factors, if none are annotatedTwo predicted values from one decoder agree by construction
Output
An association for each molecule pair, and a map of where they disagreeWhole-tissue and within-domain links answer different questions
Scored by
Partial spatial correlation within true domains, e.g., in MANTISRecommended: simulated pairs with known correlation, new specimens
Papers
SEPAR / SpaMV / MANTIS (preprint)

Task: downstream-task atlas, T25 "Cross-omics molecular association and discordance". Papers: SEPAR, Commun. Biol. 2025; SpaMV, Nat. Commun. 2026; MANTIS, preprint 2026.

This is one of four tasks tied as the most popular of type 3, with three papers. The input is two matched modalities, here RNA of gene X and its protein; the domains to condition on are the true domains annotated with the data where they exist, and otherwise the model can supply predicted domains, cell types or shared factors. Click 1: across the whole tissue, protein rises with RNA. Click 2: the blue map shows protein beyond what RNA predicts; the ringed patch has protein without RNA, which may be regulation, turnover or assay noise, and the snapshot alone cannot say which. Click 3: coloured by true domain, the link within each domain is weak; the whole-tissue trend came from domain A being high in both. It should be noted that both readings are valid but answer different questions, and that two values predicted by the same decoder agree by construction, so they cannot validate each other. SEPAR reports RNA–protein and gene–peak associations, SpaMV uses gene–protein links to read its topics, and the MANTIS preprint tests gene–metabolite links adjusted for the spatial domains annotated with the public mouse-striatum data and for cell-type proportions from deconvolution with Stereoscope: both values are regressed on them, and the leftovers are compared with a spatial correlation. (≈2:00)
02ExperimentsMethod note / Cross-omics association

Within-domain correlation: removing the domain effect

Two molecules can look linked only because both are high in the same domain; on a toy section, the two correlations are computed as follows:

As measured

  • Each dot: one spot, with its RNA of gene X and its protein X
  • Dashed line: over all spots, r = 0.92, a strong link
  • Solid lines: within domain A or B, almost flat

Domain means removed

  • Each value: minus the mean of its own domain, for RNA and for protein
  • What is left: how a spot differs from its domain
  • Line: r = 0.21, a weak link

Partial correlation

  • Defined as rpartial = corr(RNA − its domain's mean, protein − its domain's mean)
  • Question: within one domain, does a spot with more RNA have more protein?
  • Strong r, weak partial r: the domains made the link, as here
  • Both strong: the molecules also move together spot by spot
  • Groups: the true domains annotated with the data, as in MANTIS; the values stay measured
This slide explains the contrast on the cross-omics slide with a toy section of 52 spots in two domains. Left: each dot is one spot, placed by its RNA of gene X on the horizontal axis and its protein X on the vertical axis; orange spots are in domain A, which is high in both, and pink spots in domain B, which is low in both. The dashed line is the least-squares line over all spots, and the Pearson correlation over all spots is 0.92, a strong link. The solid lines are the same fit within each domain alone, and they are almost flat. Click 1: the same spots after the mean of their own domain is subtracted from both values, so each domain's cloud is moved onto zero; what is left is how a spot differs from the rest of its domain. The correlation of these leftovers is the partial correlation, 0.21, a weak link. Click 2: hence, the partial correlation is defined as the correlation of RNA minus its domain's mean with protein minus its domain's mean. It answers whether, within one domain, a spot with more RNA also has more protein. A strong whole-tissue correlation with a weak partial correlation, as here, means that the domains made the link; if both are strong, the molecules also move together spot by spot. It should be noted that both readings are valid but answer different questions, that the groups are the true domains annotated with the data, as in MANTIS, while the values stay the measured ones; if predicted domains are used instead, domains found from the same data can absorb part of a real link, so the partial correlation is then conservative. In MANTIS, the adjustment is a regression of both values on one indicator per domain, which is the same as subtracting each domain's mean, and the leftovers are then compared with a spatial correlation rather than the Pearson correlation used here. (≈2:00)
02ExperimentsType 3 / Differential accessibility

Differential accessibility: changing chromatin

Stretches of DNA that are more open, or carry more of a histone mark, in one domain are found; each is a fixed interval, e.g., a peak:

Question
Which stretches of DNA open, close or change their mark between domains?
Input / data
ATAC or histone-mark fragment counts over fixed intervalsGround truth: None in tissue; null splits and bulk chromatin data score
Input / model
Predicted domains or cell clusters as groupsA gene-level score sums a chosen window, not one interval
Output
Each interval compared between the groups, then a table of intervals with effect and adjusted evidenceOpen chromatin is not expression; H3K27me3 marks repression
Scored by
Replicate and cross-assay agreement, e.g., in the brain tri-omics atlasRecommended: random replicate splits, depth and width checks
Papers
Brain tri-omics atlas / DA benchmark (enabling)

Task: downstream-task atlas, T15 "Differential accessibility and histone-mark state analysis". Papers: brain tri-omics atlas (spatial ARP-seq and CTRP-seq), Nature 2025; differential-accessibility benchmark, Nat. Commun. 2024 (enabling).

This task asks the differential question of the chromatin: which stretches of DNA are more open, or carry more of a histone mark, in one domain than in another. The input is fragment counts over a fixed set of genomic intervals, i.e., stretches of DNA such as peaks; ATAC fragments mark open chromatin, and CUT&Tag fragments mark one histone modification, e.g., H3K27me3, a mark of repressed genes. The model supplies the predicted domains. Click 1: as in a test of gene expression, but the unit is an interval; the counts at the ringed interval are pooled per section and domain, so each section, from its own animal, is one replicate, and its spots are not. Click 2: the output is a table of intervals with effect and adjusted evidence; higher ATAC means more open, while higher H3K27me3 means more repressed. Click 3: random groups of one domain should give no calls; the DA benchmark found that many widely used single-cell tests call thousands of intervals in such null comparisons, while pseudobulk tests, i.e., tests on counts summed within each replicate, are much less prone to it. The brain tri-omics atlas tests gene-level accessibility scores, summed around each gene, between microglial subclusters, i.e., clusters predicted from its combined RNA and ATAC data of the microglial spots in lesion samples, not anatomical domains; it reports myelin-gene accessibility in the cortex by day 5 after birth, before expression at days 10 and 21, and a higher H3K27me3 score at Olig2 and Mog in a demyelinating lesion. It should be noted that open chromatin is permission, not expression, and that linking an interval to its nearest gene is a separate hypothesis. (≈2:00)
02ExperimentsMethod note / Differential accessibility

Chromatin: open DNA, histone marks and their tests

The differential-accessibility slide relies on chromatin fragments and a test per interval, which work as follows:

Open and closed DNA

  • Nucleosome: DNA wrapped on histone proteins; packed DNA is closed
  • Tn5: cuts and tags open DNA; a fragment lies between two cuts
  • Peak: an interval where fragments pile up

Histone marks

  • Mark: a chemical tag on a histone, e.g., H3K27me3 (repressive) or H3K27ac (active)
  • CUT&Tag: an antibody finds one mark, and its Tn5 cuts nearby
  • H3K27me3 often covers broad stretches, not sharp peaks

Replicates, not spots

  • Pseudobulk: counts summed per replicate, then tested
  • Null split: random groups of replicates; every call is false
  • Bias: many tests favour deep, wide or widely open peaks
This slide explains the chromatin behind the differential-accessibility slide. Left: in the nucleus, DNA is wrapped around histone proteins, and each such bead is a nucleosome; tightly packed stretches are closed, while stretches cleared of nucleosomes are open. ATAC uses the Tn5 enzyme, which cuts open DNA and attaches sequencing adapters; the piece between two cuts is a fragment, and an interval where fragments pile up is a peak. Spatial ARP-seq in the atlas does this on the tissue section. Click 1: histones also carry chemical marks. H3K27me3, i.e., three methyl groups on lysine 27 of histone H3, marks repressed genes and often covers broad stretches, while H3K27ac and H3K4me3 mark active enhancers and promoters. CUT&Tag reads one mark: an antibody binds it, and a Tn5 fused to protein A, which grips the antibody, cuts only nearby; spatial CTRP-seq in the atlas does this for H3K27me3. Click 2: the test. Spots of one section share the animal and its processing, so they are not independent; a pseudobulk test sums the counts per replicate and compares the replicates. The DA benchmark split the replicates of one cell type at random into two groups, so any call is false, and found that the most widely used single-cell tests called thousands of peaks at a false discovery rate (FDR) of 5%; these false calls came mostly from wider peaks and peaks open in more cells, and pseudobulk tests, or models with the replicate as a random effect, removed them. It should be noted that the benchmark studied single-cell ATAC, not spatial data or histone marks, and that replicates can differ for real reasons, so the null split should be repeated on each new dataset. (≈2:00)
02ExperimentsType 1 / Atlas construction

Atlas construction: one map across samples

Sections from different samples, often measured with different modalities, are integrated into one shared space and one set of labels:

Question
Can different samples share one map?
Input / data
Several sections, each with its own modality setThe atlas records which modalities each section hasGround truth: True domains, annotated by hand, used only to score; sample labels are metadata
Input / model
Anchors across sections, and predicted domainsOr a decoder conditioned on the sample
Output
A shared embedding without the sample effect, and one set of domains for all sectionsImputed values, if any, are kept apart from measured ones
Scored by
Sample mixing and agreement of predicted with true domains, e.g., in SpaMosaicRecommended: Mixing within each true domain, held-out-sample transfer, and rare states
Papers
SpaMosaic / SpaMIE / DIRAC / spaVAE family (enabling)

Task: downstream-task atlas, T05 "Cross-sample integration and atlas construction". Papers: SpaMosaic, Nat. Genet. 2026; SpaMIE, Cell Rep. Methods 2026; DIRAC, Nat. Methods 2026; spaVAE / spaPeakVAE / spaMultiVAE, Nat. Methods 2024.

The input is several sections from different samples, here measured with RNA and ATAC, RNA and protein, and RNA only; the third is a partial section. Before integration, the embedding groups spots by sample rather than by biology. Click 1: after integration, the three samples overlap, and the spots group by domain instead. Click 2: the atlas gives one set of predicted domains, the same in every section. Click 3: the score has two sides: the samples should mix within each true domain, and the domains should stay apart. DIRAC reports both, SpaMosaic builds mosaic atlases across platforms and stages, and SpaMIE evaluates multi-section embeddings. It should be noted that mixing is only good where the samples share a state: a disease state that exists in one sample must not be blended into healthy tissue to raise the mixing score. SpaMosaic and SpaMIE cluster their shared embedding into predicted domains, with mclust and Louvain, measure sample mixing with iLISI over all spots, and score the predicted domains against true domains annotated by hand, e.g., from the original studies; mixing within each true domain is our recommendation. (≈2:00)
02ExperimentsType 1 / Section registration

Section registration: aligning adjacent sections

Adjacent sections share anatomy but not cells, so one section is moved onto the other before they are compared:

Question
Where does each part lie on the next section?
Input / data
Two adjacent sections, possibly in different modalitiesRelated anatomy, but different physical cellsGround truth: Held-out landmarks, a known rotation, or true domains and cell types
Input / model
Modality-invariant embeddings and anchor pairsA soft correspondence, not one-to-one matches
Output
Matched landmarks or features, then moved coordinates and a correspondenceA rigid or affine fit, or a smooth deformation
Scored by
Recommended: error at held-out landmarks in µm and overlap of independent structuresSANTO : original cell-type labels; DIME: true domains
Papers
SANTO / DIME

Task: downstream-task atlas, T06 "Cross-section registration and correspondence". Papers: SANTO, Nat. Commun. 2024; DIME, Genome Res. 2026.

The input is two adjacent sections: A measured with RNA, B with ATAC. B holds other cells than A, and it was placed on the slide at an angle. Click 1: matched landmarks, from structures that both sections show, tell how B is turned and shifted. Click 2: B is moved onto A, and the true domains now line up. Click 3: the check uses landmarks that were not used for the fit; the small gap between each cross and its ring is the remaining error, reported in micrometres on real data. SANTO shows cross-platform, cross-modality and 3D alignment, scored against each dataset's original cell-type annotation and a known rotation, and DIME recovers domains from unaligned sections without shared features: its predicted domains are scored against true domains annotated by hand, and it reports no alignment error; the atlas notes that these are different endpoints. It should be noted that a good alignment does not mean that two sections measured the same cell, so a nearest neighbour after registration is an association, not a measurement. (≈2:00)
02ExperimentsType 1 / Anatomical gradients

Anatomical gradients: a position, not a domain

Some tissues change gradually, so each spot is given a continuous position along an anatomical axis instead of a predicted domain:

Question
Where does each spot lie along a continuous tissue axis?
Input / data
Spot profiles and positionsAxis chosen in advance, e.g., portal-to-central in liverGround truth: Held-out antibody landmarks, or true domains
Input / model
A spatially informed embeddingIts direction is set by a marker gene
Contrast
Predicted domains from domain clusteringA convenience, not proof of sharp boundaries
Output
One coordinate per niche, from 0 to 1Then cut into ordered zones; a position, not a time
Scored by
Spearman correlation and RMSE against a landmark-based axis, e.g., in LYNXRecommended: held-out markers and agreement across replicates
Papers
LYNX (preprint)

Task: downstream-task atlas, T46 "Continuous anatomical gradients and zonation". Papers: LYNX, preprint, July 2026.

This is the most novel task of type 1: its only demonstration is the LYNX preprint from July 2026. The task describes tissue that changes gradually, such as cortical depth or the portal-to-central axis of the liver. The input is a toy cortex-shaped grid of spots, with a signal that rises with depth. Click 1: domain clustering would cut it into six predicted domains, which hides the gradual change. Click 2: here each spot gets one number instead, its depth along the axis; the dashed lines join spots of equal depth. LYNX gives this number, from 0 to 1, to each niche, i.e., the neighbourhood around a cell, held at the resolution of the coarser modality; a marker gene sets which end is 0, and the number is then cut into four ordered zones. Click 3: the predicted depth is compared with the true axis built from landmarks, i.e., positions known without the model, such as the portal and central veins in liver. In LYNX, this axis is solved from the veins outward with a reaction-diffusion equation, on antibody images taken from the same section after the other measurements; these held-out data are kept away from fitting and used only to score. LYNX reports Spearman correlation and RMSE against this proxy axis for itself and six other methods, e.g., SpatialGlue and GASTON, as box plots without exact values in the text. It should be noted that a high coordinate means farther along the axis, not older or more active, and the axis must not be tuned on the same markers used to score it. LYNX is a preprint, so this is the thinnest evidence of group 1. (≈2:15)
02ExperimentsMethod note / Anatomical gradients

Spearman correlation and RMSE: order and error

The gradient slide scored the predicted axis with two numbers, which are read as follows:

  • Spearman correlation: is the order right? Perfect order is best, and a reversed order is worst
  • RMSE: how far off, in the units of the true axis? Zero is best
  • B has the right order but the wrong scale, so both scores are reported
This slide explains the two scores of the gradient slide, using three predictions of the same true axis. A sits on the dashed diagonal, so it is best on both scores. B keeps the order but bends away from the diagonal, so Spearman is still perfect while RMSE is large. C has lost the order, so Spearman falls to no link and RMSE is the largest. On the right, the letters show where each prediction falls on the two scales. It should be noted that an axis with no fixed scale, such as the gradient, is fairly scored by rank alone, whereas a predicted protein level needs both scores. (≈1:30)
02ExperimentsTakeaways

Takeaways: what a sound downstream experiment needs

Across the tasks that fit our model, the same five checks recur, and one gap stands out:

1 / Ground truth

Score against a truth the model never saw

True domains, held-out counts, landmarks or a new section score a result, but never shape it.

Atlas / registration / uncertainty
2 / Predictions

A predicted value is not a measurement

Decoder outputs and smoothed values agree by construction, so they are checked against measured data.

Uncertainty / cross-omics
3 / Circularity

Keep the test from being circular

Domains found from the same counts build in the differences, and neighbouring spots are not independent.

Differential accessibility / cross-omics
4 / Choices

Fix the choices before the results

Cut-offs, roots and the result to explain are set in advance, not tuned to what looks best.

Uncertainty / trajectories / modality contribution
5 / Baselines

Beat a simple baseline

A single-modality model, a random score or a distance-only cost shows what integration adds.

Uncertainty / retrieval / modality contribution
Gap / Coverage

Some outputs are not saved yet

Reconstructions and the leave-one-out route are computed but not saved, and are in reduced space.

Type 2: denoising and imputation
This slide collects what the task slides of this version have in common. First, every result is scored against a truth the model never saw, e.g., true domains from expert labels, held-out counts, landmarks or a new section; ground truth scores a result but never shapes it. Second, a predicted value is not a measurement: decoder outputs and smoothed values agree by construction, so they are checked against measured data. Click 1: third, a test must not be circular; domains found from the same counts build in the differences, and neighbouring spots are not independent measurements. Fourth, the choices, i.e., cut-offs, the root of a trajectory and the result a modality should explain, are fixed before the results are seen. Click 2: fifth, a method should beat a simple baseline, e.g., a single-modality model, a random uncertainty score or a transport cost from distances alone, which shows what integration adds. Finally, the gap: our model computes the decoder reconstructions, the leave-one-out reconstructions and the variance of the joint embedding, but saves none of them; with the current best configurations the reconstructions are in the reduced space, e.g., principal components, so denoising and imputation, the type 2 tasks, are left out until the reconstructions are saved and mapped back to measured features. Type 5 needs data we do not have. Overall, this suggests that the tasks of types 4 and 6 that read saved outputs, i.e., transport maps, modality weights and per-modality embeddings, are the ones our model can run first. (≈1:45)

AAppendixGlossary

Glossary: terms used on the task slides

As a backup for questions, each term below is used on at least one task slide, whose task is named under its definition:

Held-out data
Data kept away from fitting, tuning and model choice, and used only to scoreRegistration, fate mapping, uncertainty
Ground truth
An independent reference, e.g., true domains from expert labels or landmarks; it scores a result but never shapes itAtlas, registration, gradients
Domainpredicted or true
A part of the tissue whose spots share a profile; predicted when a model finds it, true when it comes from ground truthAtlas, gradients, differential tests, cross-omics
Marker
A molecule higher in one domain than in the rest of the tissueGradients
Embeddingalso called latent code
A short vector per spot learned from its profiles; nearby vectors mean similar spotsMost tasks
Partial correlation
The correlation of two features after each domain's mean is removed from both; it asks whether they move together within a domainCross-omics
Transport plan
How much of each spot of one section is sent to each spot of another, at the lowest total cost in the embeddingRegistration, fate mapping
Ablation
The model retrained without one input, e.g., a modality, to measure the score it losesModality contribution
Pseudobulk
Counts summed per replicate before a test, so replicates, not spots, are the units comparedDifferential accessibility
Modality
One kind of measurement per spot, e.g., RNA, ATAC or proteinAll tasks
Spearman correlation
The agreement of two orders; 1 means a predicted axis ranks spots exactly as the true axis, and −1 means reversedGradients
Landmark
A position known without the model, e.g., a central vein in liver; it orients and scores an axisGradients, registration
Adjusted evidence
A p-value corrected for testing many features at once, e.g., a false discovery rateDifferential accessibility
Circular test
Testing features between predicted domains found from the same data; the differences are partly built inCross-omics
Calibration
Whether stated intervals hold the true value as often as they claimUncertainty maps
Pseudotime
A spot's rank along an inferred process from a chosen root; it orders spots but is not a clockTrajectories
Modality weight
How much each modality counts when one spot's embeddings are combined into oneModality contribution
Uncertainty score
One number per spot, higher means less certain; it ranks spots and is not a probabilityUncertainty maps
This backup slide collects the terms that the task slides use. The left column is about how data are split and represented: held-out data are never used for fitting, ground truth only scores, a domain is predicted by a model or true from ground truth, a marker is a molecule higher in one domain than in the rest, and a partial correlation removes each domain's mean before two features are compared. The embedding is the short vector each spot gets. A transport plan says how much of each spot of one section goes to each spot of another, an ablation retrains a model without one input, and a pseudobulk test sums counts per replicate so that replicates, not spots, are compared. The right column starts with modality, one kind of measurement, and is otherwise about the statistics: a Spearman correlation asks whether a predicted order is right, landmarks anchor a gradient axis, adjusted evidence corrects for testing thousands of genes, a circular test reuses the data that found the domains, calibration asks whether stated intervals hold the true value as often as claimed, pseudotime is a rank along a process, a modality weight says how much each modality counts in the combined embedding, and an uncertainty score ranks spots by how certain they are. It should be noted that the methods with a picture are explained right after the first task that uses them; this slide is only for questions. (backup)
